{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_0119BQvyRsfUHFqPdWKyvkNq","type":"tool_result","content":"1	/-
2	# Rule 30 — core definitions
3	
4	An *elementary cellular automaton* is about as small as a dynamical system
5	gets: a bi-infinite row of black/white cells, updated in lock-step by a rule
6	that looks only at each cell and its two neighbours.
7	
8	This file defines all 256 of them from a rule number, specialises to rule 30,
9	and proves the one bridging lemma (`rule30_eq`) that every downstream proof
10	uses.
11	-/
12	import Mathlib.Data.Int.Notation
13	import Mathlib.Logic.Function.Iterate
14	import Mathlib.Data.Fintype.Card
15	import Mathlib.Data.Fintype.Pi
16	import Mathlib.Data.Finset.Card
17	import Mathlib.Order.Lattice.Nat
18	
19	/-- A configuration of the automaton: a bi-infinite row of cells, each black
20	(`true`) or white (`false`), indexed by the integers.
21	
22	In TypeScript terms this is exactly `(i: bigint) => boolean`. There is no
23	array, no bound, and no "edge of the world" — the row really is the function.
24	-/
25	abbrev Config : Type := ℤ → Bool
26	
27	namespace ElementaryCA
28	
29	/-- The neighbourhood of a cell, packed into the 3-bit number Wolfram numbers
30	his rules by: `left` is the high bit (4), `center` the middle bit (2), `right`
31	the low bit (1). So the all-black neighbourhood `111` is index `7`, and the
32	all-white one `000` is index `0`.
33	
34	`Bool.toNat` is the obvious `false ↦ 0`, `true ↦ 1`. -/
35	def neighborhoodIndex (left center right : Bool) : Nat :=
36	  4 * left.toNat + 2 * center.toNat + right.toNat
37	
38	/-- One step of the elementary cellular automaton with rule number `r`.
39	
40	A rule number *is* its own lookup table. Three neighbours give 8 possible
41	neighbourhoods, and the rule must supply one output bit for each — so a rule is
42	exactly one byte, and `Fin 256` is that byte. `Fin 256` carries the proof of
43	its own bound with it, so `step 300` is not a runtime error, it is unwritable.
44	
45	`Nat.testBit r.val k` reads bit `k` of the rule number, which is the output for
46	neighbourhood `k`. -/
47	def step (r : Fin 256) (c : Config) (i : ℤ) : Bool :=
48	  r.val.testBit (neighborhoodIndex (c (i - 1)) (c i) (c (i + 1)))
49	
50	end ElementaryCA
51	
52	/-- Rule 30, the automaton the Wolfram prizes are about.
53	
54	This is a *partial application*, not a wrapper: `ElementaryCA.step` takes a rule
55	first, so `ElementaryCA.step 30` is already a value of type `Config → Config`.
56	(Every Lean function takes exactly one argument, so there is no such thing as
57	"calling `step` with a missing argument" — currying is not opt-in here.) -/
58	def rule30 : Config → Config := ElementaryCA.step 30
59	
60	/-- The initial configuration the prize questions are stated against: a single
61	black cell at the origin on an infinite white background.
62	
63	`decide (i = 0)` turns the *proposition* `i = 0` into the `Bool` that says
64	whether it holds; the two are different things in Lean, and only the `Bool` can
65	be stored in a cell. -/
66	def initialConfig : Config := fun i => decide (i = 0)
67	
68	/-- The configuration after `t` steps of rule 30, starting from
69	`initialConfig`.
70	
71	`f^[t]` is `Nat.iterate`: `f` composed with itself `t` times. `rule30^[0]` is
72	the identity, so `evolve 0 = initialConfig`. -/
73	def evolve (t : Nat) : Config := rule30^[t] initialConfig
74	
75	/-- The center column: the colour of the origin cell after `t` steps.
76	
77	This single sequence of bits is the subject of all three Rule 30 Prize
78	questions (see `Rule30/Prize.lean`). It is OEIS A051023. -/
79	def centerColumn (t : Nat) : Bool := evolve t 0
80	
81	/-- The `k`-th diagonal in from the **left** edge of the cone, read `j` steps
82	along it: the cell at position `-j` after `j + k` steps. `leftDiagonal 0` is
83	the left edge itself, `leftDiagonal 1` the cells just inside it, and so on.
84	
85	In TypeScript terms it is a re-indexing, `(k, j) => evolve(j + k)(-j)`, and
86	nothing more — no new data, only a coordinate system in which the left side
87	of the pattern reads as a family of one-dimensional sequences. -/
88	def leftDiagonal (k j : Nat) : Bool := evolve (j + k) (-(j : ℤ))
89	
90	/-- The `k`-th diagonal in from the **right** edge, read `j` steps along it:
91	the cell at position `j` after `j + k` steps. Not the mirror image of
92	`leftDiagonal`: rule 30 is not left-right symmetric, and the two families
93	behave differently. -/
94	def rightDiagonal (k j : Nat) : Bool := evolve (j + k) (j : ℤ)
95	
96	/-- `f` repeats with period `p` from index `N` on: `f (n + p) = f n` for every
97	`n ≥ N`. The prefix before `N` is unconstrained.
98	
99	`IsEventuallyPeriodic f` in `Rule30/Prize.lean` is `∃ p > 0, ∃ N, PeriodicFrom
100	f p N`, written out; that file keeps the unfolded form so the prize statement
101	reads on its own. Note `p = 0` makes this trivially true, so a statement that
102	means "genuinely periodic" must carry `0 < p` alongside it. -/
103	def PeriodicFrom (f : Nat → Bool) (p N : Nat) : Prop := ∀ n ≥ N, f (n + p) = f n
104	
105	/-- **The bridging lemma.** Rule 30 in closed form: the new cell is the left
106	neighbour XOR (centre OR right neighbour).
107	
108	This is the identity every downstream proof — and the BigInt explorer's
109	`(x <<< 1) ^^^ (x ||| (x >>> 1))` — actually works with. Going from the lookup
110	table to this formula is pure case analysis: `cases` on each of the three
111	Booleans gives 8 goals, and each one is a concrete `Nat.testBit 30 k` that the
112	kernel simply computes. -/
113	theorem rule30_eq (c : Config) (i : ℤ) :
114	    rule30 c i = xor (c (i - 1)) (c i || c (i + 1)) := by
115	  show ElementaryCA.step 30 c i = _
116	  unfold ElementaryCA.step ElementaryCA.neighborhoodIndex
117	  cases c (i - 1) <;> cases c i <;> cases c (i + 1) <;> rfl
118	
119	/-- `evolve` unfolded one step, so that `rule30_eq` can be applied to it. -/
120	theorem evolve_succ (t : Nat) : evolve (t + 1) = rule30 (evolve t) := by
121	  simp [evolve, Function.iterate_succ_apply']
122	
123	/-! ## Arbitrary rows
124	
125	Everything above grows the picture from one black cell. The tools the
126	literature uses on the columns question — left-permutivity, preimage
127	counting — are about *any* starting row, so here the same picture is grown
128	from an arbitrary `c : Config`. `evolve t` is the special case
129	`evolveFrom initialConfig t`, and the two are equal by definition. -/
130	
131	/-- The row after `t` steps of rule 30, starting from any row `c`.
132	
133	The same `f^[t]` iterate as `evolve`, with the starting row a parameter
134	instead of the fixed `initialConfig`. In TypeScript this is the difference
135	between `evolve(t)` and `evolveFrom(c, t)` where the first is
136	`evolveFrom(initialConfig, t)` by definition. -/
137	def evolveFrom (c : Config) (t : Nat) : Config := rule30^[t] c
138	
139	/-- Column `i` of the picture grown from `c`: the colour of position `i`
140	after `t` steps, as a function of `t`. `centerColumn` is `column initialConfig 0`. -/
141	def column (c : Config) (i : ℤ) (t : Nat) : Bool := evolveFrom c t i
142	
143	/-- The cells of `c` at positions `-t .. t`, as a function on the finite type
144	`Fin (2 * t + 1)`: index `k` reads position `k - t`.
145	
146	The point of a *finite* type is counting. `Fin n → Bool` has `2 ^ n`
147	inhabitants and Mathlib knows it (`Fintype`), so "all windows of width
148	`2t + 1`" is `Finset.univ` and can be filtered and counted. A `Config` is
149	`ℤ → Bool` and has no such thing. -/
150	def window (c : Config) (t : Nat) : Fin (2 * t + 1) → Bool :=
151	  fun k => c ((k : ℤ) - (t : ℤ))
152	
153	/-- A window extended by white cells outside `-t .. t`, back to a full row.
154	`window (ofWindow w) t = w`, and the picture grown from `ofWindow w` agrees
155	at the origin for `t` steps with the picture grown from any row whose
156	window is `w` (that is the cone lemma, `evolveFrom_eq_of_agree_on_window`). -/
157	def ofWindow {t : Nat} (w : Fin (2 * t + 1) → Bool) : Config :=
158	  fun i => if h : 0 ≤ i + t ∧ i + t < 2 * t + 1 then w ⟨(i + t).toNat, by omega⟩ else false
159	
160	/-- `f` is **left-permutive** with radius `r`: two rows that agree at every
161	position `i - r + 1 .. i + r` and differ at `i - r` are sent to rows that
162	differ at `i`. Flipping the leftmost cell that a step reads always flips its
163	output, whatever the other cells hold.
164	
165	This is the property everything about rule 30's columns leans on. For one
166	step of rule 30 it is `rule30_eq` read as "`xor` with the left neighbour":
167	`rule30_leftPermutive`. For `t` steps it is `evolveFrom_leftPermutive`, with
168	radius `t`. -/
169	def LeftPermutive (f : Config → Config) (r : Nat) : Prop :=
170	  ∀ (c d : Config) (i : ℤ),
171	    (∀ j : ℤ, i - r < j → j ≤ i + r → c j = d j) → c (i - r) ≠ d (i - r) → f c i ≠ f d i
172	
173	/-- How many of the `2 ^ (2t + 1)` windows of width `2t + 1` grow a black
174	centre cell after `t` steps. `window_count_half` says it is exactly half. -/
175	def blackWindowCount (t : Nat) : Nat :=
176	  (Finset.univ.filter fun w : Fin (2 * t + 1) → Bool =>
177	    evolveFrom (ofWindow w) t 0 = true).card
178	
179	/-- The single-seed picture is the general one grown from `initialConfig`. -/
180	theorem evolve_eq_evolveFrom_initial (t : Nat) :
181	    evolve t = evolveFrom initialConfig t := rfl
182	
183	/-- The centre column is column `0` of the single-seed picture. -/
184	theorem centerColumn_eq_column (t : Nat) :
185	    centerColumn t = column initialConfig 0 t := rfl
186	
187	/-- `evolveFrom` unfolded one step, the way `evolve_succ` unfolds `evolve`, so
188	that `rule30_eq` can be applied to the picture grown from any row. -/
189	theorem evolveFrom_succ (c : Config) (t : Nat) :
190	    evolveFrom c (t + 1) = rule30 (evolveFrom c t) := by
191	  simp [evolveFrom, Function.iterate_succ_apply']
192	
193	/-! ## The row model
194	
195	A row of the single-seed picture has at most `2t + 1` cells, so it fits in
196	one natural number, and one step of rule 30 is three big-integer operations.
197	Lean's kernel evaluates `Nat` arithmetic with built-in bignums, so `decide`
198	can compute row 5000 in a second where evaluating `evolve` cell by cell
199	gives out near row 18. `rowCell_eq_evolve` (a node on the board) says the
200	model and the definition agree; after it, a concrete fact about any row to
201	depth in the thousands is a theorem by `decide`, with no extra axiom. -/
202	
203	/-- **Rule 30's row map, on a whole row at once.** Not to be confused with
204	`step` above, which is the general elementary-CA step on a `Config`; this is
205	rule 30 specifically, on a row packed into one `Nat`.
206	
207	`4 * r` shifts the row two
208	bits up so that bit `b` of it is the *left* neighbour of position `b - t - 1`;
209	`2 * r` is the centre; `r` itself is the right neighbour; and the whole
210	expression is `left XOR (centre OR right)`, which is `rule30_eq` applied to
211	every bit simultaneously. The explorer's BigInt engine does the same thing
212	with shifts. -/
213	def rowStep (r : Nat) : Nat := (4 * r) ^^^ ((2 * r) ||| r)
214	
215	/-- **The row map truncated to `n` bits.** `rowStep` carries information only
216	upward through the bits, so cutting to `n` bits before and after the step
217	gives the same answer as cutting after: `stepMod n` is a genuine map on
218	`Nat`s below `2 ^ n`, and the truncations form a tower rather than a
219	sequence of unrelated finite systems.
220	
221	Reading the picture: bit `k` of the row is the cell `k` places in from the
222	black left edge, so truncating to `n` bits is looking at the leftmost `n`
223	diagonals and ignoring everything further in. -/
224	def stepMod (n r : Nat) : Nat := rowStep r % 2 ^ n
225	
226	/-- Row `t` of the single-seed picture as one number: the cell at position
227	`x` is bit `x + t`, so bit `0` is the left edge and bit `2t` the right edge.
228	
229	The step is `rule30_eq` on all bits at once. `4 * r` shifts the row two bits
230	up so that bit `b` of it is the *left* neighbour of position `b - t - 1`;
231	`2 * r` is the centre; `r` itself is the right neighbour; and
232	`(4 * r) ^^^ ((2 * r) ||| r)` is `left XOR (centre OR right)`. The explorer's
233	BigInt engine does the same thing with shifts. -/
234	def rowNat : Nat → Nat
235	  | 0 => 1
236	  | t + 1 => let r := rowNat t; (4 * r) ^^^ ((2 * r) ||| r)
237	
238	/-- The cell at position `x` of row `t`, read from `rowNat`; white outside
239	the cone `-t .. t`, where the number has no bit for it. -/
240	def rowCell (t : Nat) (x : ℤ) : Bool :=
241	  if -(t : ℤ) ≤ x ∧ x ≤ t then (rowNat t).testBit (x + t).toNat else false
242	
243	/-- The model agrees with `evolve` on every cell of the first seven rows. A
244	kernel computation, kept in the file as a guard against the orientation
245	error that is easy to make here (the mirror image is rule 86 and passes
246	every symmetric check). The general statement is `rowCell_eq_evolve`. -/
247	example : ∀ t : Fin 7, ∀ x : Fin 13, rowCell t ((x : ℤ) - 6) = evolve t ((x : ℤ) - 6) := by
248	  decide
249	
250	/-! ## The two half-lines and the sideways solve
251	
252	Each half of the picture is driven by the centre column alone. A cell at
253	position `x ≥ 1` reads only positions `x - 1`, `x`, `x + 1`, all `≥ 0`, so
254	the right half `x ≥ 1`, given its own row 0 and the centre column as a
255	boundary, evolves without ever looking left of the origin; the left half is
256	the mirror. And columns 0 and 1 together determine everything to their
257	left, one column per step of `sideways_inverse`. The three definitions below
258	make these views into functions of `ℕ` alone, so they can be stated and
259	computed without a `Config`; the agreement theorems in `Statements.lean`
260	tie each back to `column`.
261	
262	In TypeScript terms, `evolve` is a loop over the whole infinite row, and
263	`evolveHalfLeft c w` is the same loop over a half-open array whose closed
264	end reads `c t` instead of a neighbour. The seam is that the boundary is a
265	*given* sequence here, not something the loop computes — which is exactly
266	why the half-line can be fed a boundary that no row would produce. -/
267	
268	/-- The left half-line: `evolveHalfLeft c w t k` is the cell at position
269	`-(k + 1)` after `t` steps, grown from row 0 `w` (`w k` is the cell at
270	`-(k + 1)`) with the boundary column `c` standing in for position `0`. -/
271	def evolveHalfLeft (c w : ℕ → Bool) : ℕ → ℕ → Bool
272	  | 0, k => w k
273	  | t + 1, 0 => xor (evolveHalfLeft c w t 1) (evolveHalfLeft c w t 0 || c t)
274	  | t + 1, k + 1 =>
275	      xor (evolveHalfLeft c w t (k + 2))
276	        (evolveHalfLeft c w t (k + 1) || evolveHalfLeft c w t k)
277	
278	/-- The right half-line: `evolveHalfRight c y t k` is the cell at position
279	`k + 1` after `t` steps, grown from row 0 `y` (`y k` is the cell at `k + 1`)
280	with the boundary column `c` standing in for position `0`. -/
281	def evolveHalfRight (c y : ℕ → Bool) : ℕ → ℕ → Bool
282	  | 0, k => y k
283	  | t + 1, 0 => xor (c t) (evolveHalfRight c y t 0 || evolveHalfRight c y t 1)
284	  | t + 1, k + 1 =>
285	      xor (evolveHalfRight c y t k)
286	        (evolveHalfRight c y t (k + 1) || evolveHalfRight c y t (k + 2))
287	
288	/-- The sideways solve: `leftSolve c d k t` is the cell at position `-k` at
289	time `t`, rebuilt from column `0` (`c`) and column `1` (`d`) alone by
290	`sideways_inverse`, one column per step leftward: the cell at `-(k + 1)` is
291	the cell at `-k` one step later, XOR (the cell at `-k` OR the cell at
292	`-k + 1`). Column `1` is read only in the first step. -/
293	def leftSolve (c d : ℕ → Bool) : ℕ → ℕ → Bool
294	  | 0, t => c t
295	  | 1, t => xor (c (t + 1)) (c t || d t)
296	  | k + 2, t =>
297	      xor (leftSolve c d (k + 1) (t + 1))
298	        (leftSolve c d (k + 1) t || leftSolve c d k t)
299	
300	/-- The three models agree with the row model on the single seed for the
301	first steps. Kernel computations kept in the file as guards against an
302	orientation error (a mirrored half-line passes every symmetric check); the
303	general statements are `evolveHalfLeft_eq_column`, `evolveHalfRight_eq_column`
304	and `leftSolve_eq_column`. -/
305	example : ∀ t : Fin 8, ∀ k : Fin 8,
306	    evolveHalfLeft (fun t => rowCell t 0) (fun _ => false) t k
307	      = rowCell t (-((k : ℤ) + 1)) := by
308	  decide
309	
310	example : ∀ t : Fin 8, ∀ k : Fin 8,
311	    evolveHalfRight (fun t => rowCell t 0) (fun _ => false) t k
312	      = rowCell t ((k : ℤ) + 1) := by
313	  decide
314	
315	example : ∀ k : Fin 7, ∀ t : Fin 7,
316	    leftSolve (fun t => rowCell t 0) (fun t => rowCell t 1) k t
317	      = rowCell t (-(k : ℤ)) := by
318	  decide
319	
320	/-! ## The settled configuration
321	
322	Every left diagonal settles into a repeating word from some onset on
323	(`leftDiagonal_periodicFrom_pow`), and the settled cells form a region on
324	the left whose boundary, the seam, runs down the picture at about a quarter
325	of the way in from the centre. Read the picture down a column far to the
326	left, starting at the left edge: if the column's distance from the origin
327	is a multiple of `2 ^ k` and past the onsets, the `k`-th cell below the edge
328	is the same whichever such column is read. That common value is
329	`settledCenter k`, the centre column the picture would have if its diagonals
330	had no transients; and the row that grows the settled region without any
331	transient at all is `settledConfig`. Both are read off the seed's own
332	picture at indices past every onset: `2 ^ k` on diagonal `k`, and
333	`2 ^ (x + 1) - x` for the cell at position `x` of the settled row, which is
334	past the onset of diagonal `x` and congruent to `-x` modulo its period.
335	
336	In TypeScript terms these are memoised reads of a lazily computed table,
337	not new automata: nothing here runs rule 30 on anything but the seed. The
338	seam is that the settled row is infinite to the right, so its own picture
339	is not a cone and its column at the origin, which `column_settledConfig_eq`
340	identifies with `settledCenter`, is a new sequence with no transient. -/
341	
342	/-- The settled centre column: the settled word of diagonal `k` at index `0`,
343	read from the seed's picture at index `2 ^ k`, which is past the onset and a
344	multiple of the period. -/

# Rule 30 — core definitions

An *elementary cellular automaton* is about as small as a dynamical system
gets: a bi-infinite row of black/white cells, updated in lock-step by a rule
that looks only at each cell and its two neighbours.

This file defines all 256 of them from a rule number, specialises to rule 30,
and proves the one bridging lemma (`rule30_eq`) that every downstream proof
uses.
-/
import Mathlib.Data.Int.Notation
import Mathlib.Logic.Function.Iterate
import Mathlib.Data.Fintype.Card
import Mathlib.Data.Fintype.Pi
import Mathlib.Data.Finset.Card
import Mathlib.Order.Lattice.Nat

/-- A configuration of the automaton: a bi-infinite row of cells, each black
(`true`) or white (`false`), indexed by the integers.

In TypeScript terms this is exactly `(i: bigint) => boolean`. There is no
array, no bound, and no "edge of the world" — the row really is the function.
-/
abbrev Config : Type := ℤ → Bool

namespace ElementaryCA

/-- The neighbourhood of a cell, packed into the 3-bit number Wolfram numbers
his rules by: `left` is the high bit (4), `center` the middle bit (2), `right`
the low bit (1). So the all-black neighbourhood `111` is index `7`, and the
all-white one `000` is index `0`.

`Bool.toNat` is the obvious `false ↦ 0`, `true ↦ 1`. -/
def neighborhoodIndex (left center right : Bool) : Nat :=
  4 * left.toNat + 2 * center.toNat + right.toNat

/-- One step of the elementary cellular automaton with rule number `r`.

A rule number *is* its own lookup table. Three neighbours give 8 possible
neighbourhoods, and the rule must supply one output bit for each — so a rule is
exactly one byte, and `Fin 256` is that byte. `Fin 256` carries the proof of
its own bound with it, so `step 300` is not a runtime error, it is unwritable.

`Nat.testBit r.val k` reads bit `k` of the rule number, which is the output for
neighbourhood `k`. -/
def step (r : Fin 256) (c : Config) (i : ℤ) : Bool :=
  r.val.testBit (neighborhoodIndex (c (i - 1)) (c i) (c (i + 1)))

end ElementaryCA

/-- Rule 30, the automaton the Wolfram prizes are about.

This is a *partial application*, not a wrapper: `ElementaryCA.step` takes a rule
first, so `ElementaryCA.step 30` is already a value of type `Config → Config`.
(Every Lean function takes exactly one argument, so there is no such thing as
"calling `step` with a missing argument" — currying is not opt-in here.) -/
def rule30 : Config → Config := ElementaryCA.step 30

/-- The initial configuration the prize questions are stated against: a single
black cell at the origin on an infinite white background.

`decide (i = 0)` turns the *proposition* `i = 0` into the `Bool` that says
whether it holds; the two are different things in Lean, and only the `Bool` can
be stored in a cell. -/
def initialConfig : Config := fun i => decide (i = 0)

/-- The configuration after `t` steps of rule 30, starting from
`initialConfig`.

`f^[t]` is `Nat.iterate`: `f` composed with itself `t` times. `rule30^[0]` is
the identity, so `evolve 0 = initialConfig`. -/
def evolve (t : Nat) : Config := rule30^[t] initialConfig

/-- The center column: the colour of the origin cell after `t` steps.

This single sequence of bits is the subject of all three Rule 30 Prize
questions (see `Rule30/Prize.lean`). It is OEIS A051023. -/
def centerColumn (t : Nat) : Bool := evolve t 0

/-- The `k`-th diagonal in from the **left** edge of the cone, read `j` steps
along it: the cell at position `-j` after `j + k` steps. `leftDiagonal 0` is
the left edge itself, `leftDiagonal 1` the cells just inside it, and so on.

In TypeScript terms it is a re-indexing, `(k, j) => evolve(j + k)(-j)`, and
nothing more — no new data, only a coordinate system in which the left side
of the pattern reads as a family of one-dimensional sequences. -/
def leftDiagonal (k j : Nat) : Bool := evolve (j + k) (-(j : ℤ))

/-- The `k`-th diagonal in from the **right** edge, read `j` steps along it:
the cell at position `j` after `j + k` steps. Not the mirror image of
`leftDiagonal`: rule 30 is not left-right symmetric, and the two families
behave differently. -/
def rightDiagonal (k j : Nat) : Bool := evolve (j + k) (j : ℤ)

/-- `f` repeats with period `p` from index `N` on: `f (n + p) = f n` for every
`n ≥ N`. The prefix before `N` is unconstrained.

`IsEventuallyPeriodic f` in `Rule30/Prize.lean` is `∃ p > 0, ∃ N, PeriodicFrom

reads on its own. Note `p = 0` makes this trivially true, so a statement that
means "genuinely periodic" must carry `0 < p` alongside it. -/
def PeriodicFrom (f : Nat → Bool) (p N : Nat) : Prop := ∀ n ≥ N, f (n + p) = f n

neighbour XOR (centre OR right neighbour).

This is the identity every downstream proof — and the BigInt explorer's
`(x <<< 1) ^^^ (x ||| (x >>> 1))` — actually works with. Going from the lookup

theorem rule30_eq (c : Config) (i : ℤ) :
    rule30 c i = xor (c (i - 1)) (c i || c (i + 1)) := by
  show ElementaryCA.step 30 c i = _
  unfold ElementaryCA.step ElementaryCA.neighborhoodIndex
  cases c (i - 1) <;> cases c i <;> cases c (i + 1) <;> rfl

theorem evolve_succ (t : Nat) : evolve (t + 1) = rule30 (evolve t) := by
  simp [evolve, Function.iterate_succ_apply']

Everything above grows the picture from one black cell. The tools the
literature uses on the columns question — left-permutivity, preimage
counting — are about *any* starting row, so here the same picture is grown
from an arbitrary `c : Config`. `evolve t` is the special case
`evolveFrom initialConfig t`, and the two are equal by definition. -/

/-- The row after `t` steps of rule 30, starting from any row `c`.

The same `f^[t]` iterate as `evolve`, with the starting row a parameter
instead of the fixed `initialConfig`. In TypeScript this is the difference
between `evolve(t)` and `evolveFrom(c, t)` where the first is
`evolveFrom(initialConfig, t)` by definition. -/
def evolveFrom (c : Config) (t : Nat) : Config := rule30^[t] c

/-- Column `i` of the picture grown from `c`: the colour of position `i`
after `t` steps, as a function of `t`. `centerColumn` is `column initialConfig 0`. -/
def column (c : Config) (i : ℤ) (t : Nat) : Bool := evolveFrom c t i

/-- The cells of `c` at positions `-t .. t`, as a function on the finite type
`Fin (2 * t + 1)`: index `k` reads position `k - t`.

The point of a *finite* type is counting. `Fin n → Bool` has `2 ^ n`
inhabitants and Mathlib knows it (`Fintype`), so "all windows of width
`2t + 1`" is `Finset.univ` and can be filtered and counted. A `Config` is
`ℤ → Bool` and has no such thing. -/
def window (c : Config) (t : Nat) : Fin (2 * t + 1) → Bool :=
  fun k => c ((k : ℤ) - (t : ℤ))

/-- A window extended by white cells outside `-t .. t`, back to a full row.
`window (ofWindow w) t = w`, and the picture grown from `ofWindow w` agrees
at the origin for `t` steps with the picture grown from any row whose
window is `w` (that is the cone lemma, `evolveFrom_eq_of_agree_on_window`). -/
def ofWindow {t : Nat} (w : Fin (2 * t + 1) → Bool) : Config :=
  fun i => if h : 0 ≤ i + t ∧ i + t < 2 * t + 1 then w ⟨(i + t).toNat, by omega⟩ else false

/-- `f` is **left-permutive** with radius `r`: two rows that agree at every
position `i - r + 1 .. i + r` and differ at `i - r` are sent to rows that
differ at `i`. Flipping the leftmost cell that a step reads always flips its
output, whatever the other cells hold.

This is the property everything about rule 30's columns leans on. For one
step of rule 30 it is `rule30_eq` read as "`xor` with the left neighbour":
`rule30_leftPermutive`. For `t` steps it is `evolveFrom_leftPermutive`, with
radius `t`. -/
def LeftPermutive (f : Config → Config) (r : Nat) : Prop :=
  ∀ (c d : Config) (i : ℤ),
    (∀ j : ℤ, i - r < j → j ≤ i + r → c j = d j) → c (i - r) ≠ d (i - r) → f c i ≠ f d i

/-- How many of the `2 ^ (2t + 1)` windows of width `2t + 1` grow a black
centre cell after `t` steps. `window_count_half` says it is exactly half. -/
def blackWindowCount (t : Nat) : Nat :=
  (Finset.univ.filter fun w : Fin (2 * t + 1) → Bool =>
    evolveFrom (ofWindow w) t 0 = true).card

/-- The single-seed picture is the general one grown from `initialConfig`. -/
theorem evolve_eq_evolveFrom_initial (t : Nat) :
    evolve t = evolveFrom initialConfig t := rfl

/-- The centre column is column `0` of the single-seed picture. -/
theorem centerColumn_eq_column (t : Nat) :
    centerColumn t = column initialConfig 0 t := rfl

/-- `evolveFrom` unfolded one step, the way `evolve_succ` unfolds `evolve`, so
that `rule30_eq` can be applied to the picture grown from any row. -/
theorem evolveFrom_succ (c : Config) (t : Nat) :
    evolveFrom c (t + 1) = rule30 (evolveFrom c t) := by
  simp [evolveFrom, Function.iterate_succ_apply']

/-! ## The row model

A row of the single-seed picture has at most `2t + 1` cells, so it fits in
one natural number, and one step of rule 30 is three big-integer operations.
Lean's kernel evaluates `Nat` arithmetic with built-in bignums, so `decide`
can compute row 5000 in a second where evaluating `evolve` cell by cell
gives out near row 18. `rowCell_eq_evolve` (a node on the board) says the
model and the definition agree; after it, a concrete fact about any row to
depth in the thousands is a theorem by `decide`, with no extra axiom. -/

/-- **Rule 30's row map, on a whole row at once.** Not to be confused with
`step` above, which is the general elementary-CA step on a `Config`; this is
rule 30 specifically, on a row packed into one `Nat`.

`4 * r` shifts the row two
bits up so that bit `b` of it is the *left* neighbour of position `b - t - 1`;
`2 * r` is the centre; `r` itself is the right neighbour; and the whole
expression is `left XOR (centre OR right)`, which is `rule30_eq` applied to
every bit simultaneously. The explorer's BigInt engine does the same thing
with shifts. -/
def rowStep (r : Nat) : Nat := (4 * r) ^^^ ((2 * r) ||| r)

/-- **The row map truncated to `n` bits.** `rowStep` carries information only
upward through the bits, so cutting to `n` bits before and after the step
gives the same answer as cutting after: `stepMod n` is a genuine map on
`Nat`s below `2 ^ n`, and the truncations form a tower rather than a
sequence of unrelated finite systems.

Reading the picture: bit `k` of the row is the cell `k` places in from the
black left edge, so truncating to `n` bits is looking at the leftmost `n`
diagonals and ignoring everything further in. -/
def stepMod (n r : Nat) : Nat := rowStep r % 2 ^ n

/-- Row `t` of the single-seed picture as one number: the cell at position
`x` is bit `x + t`, so bit `0` is the left edge and bit `2t` the right edge.

The step is `rule30_eq` on all bits at once. `4 * r` shifts the row two bits
up so that bit `b` of it is the *left* neighbour of position `b - t - 1`;
`2 * r` is the centre; `r` itself is the right neighbour; and
`(4 * r) ^^^ ((2 * r) ||| r)` is `left XOR (centre OR right)`. The explorer's
BigInt engine does the same thing with shifts. -/
def rowNat : Nat → Nat
  | 0 => 1
  | t + 1 => let r := rowNat t; (4 * r) ^^^ ((2 * r) ||| r)

/-- The cell at position `x` of row `t`, read from `rowNat`; white outside
the cone `-t .. t`, where the number has no bit for it. -/
def rowCell (t : Nat) (x : ℤ) : Bool :=
  if -(t : ℤ) ≤ x ∧ x ≤ t then (rowNat t).testBit (x + t).toNat else false

/-! ## The two half-lines and the sideways solve

Each half of the picture is driven by the centre column alone. A cell at
position `x ≥ 1` reads only positions `x - 1`, `x`, `x + 1`, all `≥ 0`, so
the right half `x ≥ 1`, given its own row 0 and the centre column as a
boundary, evolves without ever looking left of the origin; the left half is
the mirror. And columns 0 and 1 together determine everything to their
left, one column per step of `sideways_inverse`. The three definitions below
make these views into functions of `ℕ` alone, so they can be stated and
computed without a `Config`; the agreement theorems in `Statements.lean`

*given* sequence here, not something the loop computes — which is exactly
why the half-line can be fed a boundary that no row would produce. -/

/-- The left half-line: `evolveHalfLeft c w t k` is the cell at position
`-(k + 1)` after `t` steps, grown from row 0 `w` (`w k` is the cell at
`-(k + 1)`) with the boundary column `c` standing in for position `0`. -/
def evolveHalfLeft (c w : ℕ → Bool) : ℕ → ℕ → Bool
  | 0, k => w k
  | t + 1, 0 => xor (evolveHalfLeft c w t 1) (evolveHalfLeft c w t 0 || c t)
  | t + 1, k + 1 =>
      xor (evolveHalfLeft c w t (k + 2))

with the boundary column `c` standing in for position `0`. -/

  | 0, k => y k
  | t + 1, 0 => xor (c t) (evolveHalfRight c y t 0 || evolveHalfRight c y t 1)
  | t + 1, k + 1 =>

/-!
Groma, 2026-09-10 — a kernel check of the gap rule of the sighting's §3.1,
against the board's own `rowCell` model rather than against my JavaScript.

`gapAt t` is the least `x ≥ 1` with `rowCell t x = true` (0 if there is none).
The claim is that `gapAt (t+1)` is determined by `(rowCell t 0, gapAt t)` in
four of the five states:

  centre white, g ≥ 2  →  g - 1        (the leftmost black walks one place left)
  centre white, g = 1  →  1            (white_run_monotone)
  centre black, g ≥ 3  →  1            (a black centre plants a black at x = 1)
  centre black, g = 2  →  2
  centre black, g = 1  →  unconstrained (the escape state)

`ok t` is `true` when the prediction holds or the state is the escape one.
-/

def firstBlack : Nat → Nat → Nat
  | _, 0 => 0
  | t, (n + 1) =>
      let x := t + 1 - (n + 1)
      if rowCell t (x : Int) then x else firstBlack t n

/-- least `x` with `1 ≤ x ≤ t` and `rowCell t x = true`, or `0` if none. -/
def gapAt (t : Nat) : Nat := firstBlack t t

def gapPred (c : Bool) (g : Nat) : Option Nat :=
  if c then (if 3 ≤ g then some 1 else if g = 2 then some 2 else none)
  else (if 2 ≤ g then some (g - 1) else some 1)

def ok (t : Nat) : Bool :=
  match gapPred (rowCell t 0) (gapAt t) with
  | none => true
  | some v => v == gapAt (t + 1)

def okWrong (t : Nat) : Bool :=
  match (if rowCell t 0 then gapPred (rowCell t 0) (gapAt t)
         else (if 2 ≤ gapAt t then some (gapAt t) else some 1)) with
  | none => true
  | some v => v == gapAt (t + 1)

-- sanity: the first gaps, read off the board's own row model
#eval (List.range 24).map gapAt
#eval (List.range 24).map (fun t => if rowCell t 0 then 1 else 0)
#eval (List.range 60).all ok
#eval (List.range 60).any (fun t => gapPred (rowCell t 0) (gapAt t) = none)
#eval (List.range 60).all okWrong

set_option maxRecDepth 100000 in
example : (List.range 60).all ok = true := by decide

-- not vacuous: the escape state occurs in the range
set_option maxRecDepth 100000 in
example : (List.range 60).any (fun t => gapPred (rowCell t 0) (gapAt t) == none) = true := by decide

-- and the check has teeth: dropping the decrement fails on the same range
set_option maxRecDepth 100000 in
example : (List.range 60).all okWrong = false := by decide
